Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY

My Lord, I recall Dr John Gibbs, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Doctor, could you state your name for the record, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. You have come today to assist us with your involvement with a baby by the name of [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall [Baby I] from her time at the neonatal unit at Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right, or are you aware, that [Baby I] spent some time within the unit as an inpatient?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right that you dealt with her on two occasions, on 21 September 2015 and 27 September 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I examined her then as part -- I was paediatrician of the week and I was doing routine ward rounds on the neonatal unit on those days.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That was during the course of one of her stays at Chester.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were aware, were you, that she -- sorry, before we move on from the 21st, did you find on the 21st and the 27th any respiratory difficulties with [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And was her physical examination normal at that time when you saw her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We've heard about a series of incidents on the 13th, the 14th and 15 October 2015. Were you involved in any of those incidents involving [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not as far as I can remember, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Are you aware she then went and spent some time at Arrowe Park Hospital?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, a couple of days, I think.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When she returned from Arrowe Park on 17 October, was [Baby I]'s condition considered to be stable?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When did you, please, next become involved with the treatment of [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As far as I can recall, it was when I was called in urgently in the very early hours of the morning of 23 October.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were you aware, when you were called in, of [Baby I]'s most recent course of progress since her return from Arrowe Park?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because we have regular handovers each time we're on call in the evening and I knew she'd been stable. People were happy with her progress. The only concern was we were not sure what was happening with her abdomen and she was awaiting transfer to Alder Hey Hospital to have an investigation of her bowel, an imaging investigation. Because of that, she was not supposed to be fed by mouth. But she was fine and from a
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: breathing point of view, which is important in premature babies, her breathing was fine at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall the time that you were asked -- you told us you were called in urgently to see [Baby I] as the on-call consultant, do you remember roughly what time that was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I know it was in the middle of the night. Having reviewed the notes, I was called at about -- I think it was 00.05, as stated in the notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you have an independent recollection of those events or have you relied to any extent on the notes that you made at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's both. I have some memory of the events. I don't remember them in absolute detail from 7 years ago. But I've reviewed them in the notes as well, the notes I took at the time or shortly after each event.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall who asked for you to come in as a matter of urgency?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Who actually phoned me, no, I don't remember. It's often switchboard, actually, who -- someone on the switchboard is asked to get hold of you urgently as a consultant on call. I found out quite quickly, either maybe at the telephone call or as soon as I arrived in the hospital, it was the registrar on call, Dr Chang, that wanted me there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Perhaps if we go to your notes, Dr Gibbs, please. Could we begin, please, at tile 108?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have access to the swipe data, as you can see, that was recorded at the time. If we click behind it, that shows us that you were arriving through the neonatal doors, I think, yes, at 00.06. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I don't remember exactly what time I arrived, but I wrote in the notes that I was called about five past and thought I'd arrived about quarter past. So obviously what I was recording in the notes is slightly different to what the door data was saying.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember where you were when you were called?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At home.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll go to the next note, please, at 110, Mr Murphy, timed at 00.45. Would that be written in retrospect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the times are being recalled in retrospect as well?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's what I've put:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Called at [and that squiggle line is meant to stand for approximately] 00.05. Arrived at 00.10 to 00.15."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But as you say, the door says I was in at 6 minutes past so those times are probably slightly inaccurate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you have any independent recollection of what you found when you arrived on the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, [Baby I] was being resuscitated at the time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And do you remember who was present at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, Dr Rachel Chang, the registrar, was there, and two of the -- there are other nurses around on the unit, but the two nurses mainly involved with [Baby I] were Staff Nurse Lucy Letby and Staff Nurse Ashleigh Hudson.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall what you were told when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That [Baby I] -- the nurses -- and I don't remember -- I think it was Ashleigh Hudson, but the nurses were telling me that she'd suddenly seemed very distressed and was making an abnormal cry. That was about 10 minutes or so before I arrived — so just before midnight, roughly -- and then she'd rapidly deteriorated, her oxygen saturation, which was being measured, dropped, and her heart rate dropped. And they were so concerned that they needed to take over her breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The usual sequence of events, and I wasn't there for it, would be the nurses or nurse with [Baby I] would have initiated the support and called the registrar, which was Dr Chang.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But that had happened before I'd arrived. But they were all there helping [Baby I] when I arrived.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. What was [Baby I]'s status with respect to ventilation when you arrived; do you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was being ventilated with a Neopuff device through an endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were you told who'd fitted that endotracheal tube and when?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It had been Rachel Chang, shortly before I arrived. And also I was told that [Baby I] had had to have chest compressions, but those had -- to help support her circulation, but those had stopped by the time I'd arrived, so it was just for a few minutes she'd needed that support, but she was continuing to need breathing support at the time I arrived.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go to your note then, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On arrival [you have noted], intubated and Neopuff ventilated."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does that say "receiving bolus of saline"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that was taking place when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You've given a description of [Baby I]. Could you take us through that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So [Baby I] was active, which meant she was moving. She had a pink-coloured face but she was pale and mottled in her trunk and peripheries. That's an indication of reduced circulation, but we would expect that giving some fluid should improve her circulation. As I said, the saline was being given at the time and as a bolus means given quite quickly. Her colour steadily improved over the next 5 minutes and then she became pink all over.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It says "mottled" -- what are the next few words, sorry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Blue"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Mottled blue trunk and peripheries."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That means her limbs and her trunk were mottled and blue.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the colour you noted is blue?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In her body, but pink in her face, yes. Then her colour improved and became pink all over.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, okay. The mottling was to the abdomen, did you say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Abdomen and limbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Colour steadily improved over next 5 minutes."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And she became pink all over?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just explain the next entry to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put in quotation marks "fighting when placed on ventilator". Fighting meaning she was active, resisting, looking as though she was fighting the ventilator. And when we ventilate patients, a patient of any age needs to cooperate with ventilation. Often they do because they're semi-conscious or unconscious because they're unwell and needing ventilation, or sometimes they've been given medication to relax them, so that they won't fight/resist the ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Otherwise ventilation becomes very difficult if a patient is trying to breathe by themselves at the same time as a ventilator's trying to breathe and often one counteracts the other.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does the fact that [Baby I] was fighting the ventilator tell you anything about her condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's a very good sign. It's usually a condition that someone's fairly well and doesn't want to be ventilated. The fact that her colour had improved and she was resisting being ventilated were good signs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does that then say underneath "good air entry"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's "good AE" for air entry and then in brackets "with own breaths", so this is -- she was actually taking her own breaths now rather than the ventilator giving her breaths and you could hear good air entry throughout her chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that "crackles"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Crackles on inspiration." So although there was good air entry all over, there were some crackles. It just means moist, likely to be some secretions in the airways, and you could hear the crackles when [Baby I] was breathing in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that "cap refill"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Cap refill, for capillary refill, is less than 2 seconds, which again is a good sign related to circulation. I hadn't recorded the capillary refill at the time a little earlier when her limbs had been mottled and blue and pale and it would have been well over 2 seconds and that's a slow, reduced circulation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: By this stage, though, after attempting to put [Baby I] on the ventilator, she was fighting the ventilator, she was pink all over, and just pressing on her skin for 5 seconds and releasing it, the skin colour returned within 2 seconds, which is a sign of normal circulation or good circulation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. And something about distension, could you tell us about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Mod [for moderate] abdo [abdominal] distension."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So her tummy was a little distended at this stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you examine her tummy at all; do you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I would have done to have written down moderately distended. I can't remember if I put my hand -- very likely I had examined [Baby I] and put my hand on her tummy, but you can see distension just visibly sometimes, so by saying moderate abdominal distension, that's normally a visual inspection, but likely I would have felt her tummy as well. And if I'd found anything abnormal on feeling her tummy, I would have normally recorded it, so I presumably didn't to have not recorded anything.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the only observation is the distension itself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a little swollen, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that "chest X-ray"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And do you recall looking at an X-ray that had been recently taken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you've noted there what you saw?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that chronic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's "chronic, thickened airway changes". So it just means that the airway -- the sort of linear lines across the chest due to the airway markings were a little more -- more prominent than usual. The reason I say chronic, meaning longstanding, is that it was a similar appearance on [Baby I]'s previous X-rays, so that hadn't changed. It's a sign of chronic lung disease of prematurity.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we just pause there, please, and if we can come away from that note and look at tile 116. So this was the X-ray taken at 00.23, which would have been before you made your note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Before I made the notes, but I would have been there when it was taken from my arrival.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Do you recall, was this the X-ray you were shown?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It looks like it and I'm just checking at the bottom, it does say -- yes, it's taken on 23/10, as you say, at 00.23.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that thickening, is that apparent as you look now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, particularly -- so the airway down -- the right airway here -- that's the airway in the centre, that's the -the white either side is the wall of the airway and you don't normally see the airways that easily. That's because [Baby I] has slight thickened airways.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And similarly on the left-hand side, it's seen through the heart shadow, you can see that sort of black line there (indicating), the equivalent to these black lines here (indicating). They show up because there's white outside that as well but you can't see that through the heart.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: These lines over here (indicating) and even the sort of cobweb appearance throughout the rest of the lungs is just more prominent lungs markings. But this is similar to [Baby I]'s previous X-rays, so that's why I say it's a chronic change, it's not a new change in her that night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And what does it mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's signs -- an appearance they have in an X-ray in a baby that's usually been ventilated for prematurity. We call it surfactant-deficient respiratory disease of prematurity, which [Baby I] had been in the first 10 days or so of her life. And she'd needed ventilation when she deteriorated at other times over the previous 11 weeks. And unfortunately, a side effect of ventilating, particularly small babies, is that it can cause some lung damage. That side effect is well worth having in order to stay alive, but it leaves some damage in the lungs and you can see that by these thickened airway markings.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it's a sign of the ventilation that she had --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Had in the past. But chronic lung disease usually improves and resolves in babies, but can take up to a year or two to resolve completely.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does it cause you as you look now and cast your mind back to 00.25 on 23 October, did it cause you any great concern at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, because it's the same as on a previous X-ray, so there hadn't been any new change. The reason to do the X-rays is to try and understand why [Baby I] had suddenly collapsed just before midnight.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we return to the note, please. It was 110. "In view of vigorous movement", is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you take us through that part of your note, pease?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "In view of vigorous movements and resisting ventilation, decided to extubate (rather than morphine and paralysis to facilitate ventilation)."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So this was my decision on what to do with [Baby I] next to support her. Often, when a baby has deteriorated and needed help with breathing to the extent of needing an endotracheal tube inserting, the disorder or disease that would have caused that deterioration doesn't go away suddenly and the endotracheal tube needs to stay in the windpipe and a baby would need to continue ventilating.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Unusually, [Baby I] was behaving very differently: she was vigorous, active, fighting, resisting the ventilation, her
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: circulation had improved. So a baby in that state, if you're going to continue ventilation, you have to sedate them, and [Baby I] was being so vigorous that I felt she would not just need sedation, which would be the morphine, sedation and pain relief, she'd need paralysis as well, which is what indeed she'd had in the past when she'd a deterioration and needed longerterm ventilation for several days. But she was looking so good and I couldn't understand what natural disease would have caused her deterioration and yet she's recovered so rapidly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So either I had to knock her out, sedate her heavily, paralyse her, and carry on ventilating her or take the endotracheal tube out and see how she managed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Given her vigorous active state, I decided to take the endotracheal tube -- well, I asked Dr Chang, I think it was, to take it out.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just before we move on from that point, what you could see for yourself, her vigorous movements in comparison to what you knew had happened half an hour or so before --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- you said it didn't -- you didn't understand, you expected, did you, that that continuing (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Babies collapse because something has affected them. And usually it'd be some sort of disease process. It's true that sometimes babies can deteriorate -- premature babies can deteriorate very quickly. Usually we'd hope to have some warning that they were deteriorating; that's why we monitor and perform observations on babies. In [Baby I]'s case, so I was told, she'd been fine up to just before midnight, her breathing had been fine, her tummy had been soft and not distended, so she had rapidly deteriorated shortly before midnight.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But although some diseases, some disorders, can come on quickly -- and the common disorders will be infection or haemorrhage or necrotising enterocolitis, a problem we'd wondered about in [Baby I] during her 11 weeks on the unit, or severe lung disease -- it can sometimes deteriorate and come on quickly, but once you have deteriorated to the extent of needing ventilating it's not going to go away suddenly. And so a child should be -- I expected [Baby I] to be floppy, unresponsive, not resisting being ventilated. So I couldn't understand what natural disease had affected her that she'd recovered so quickly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that decision to extubate, was that taken in consultation with anybody else? Did you discuss it with any other clinician?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I would always normally -- I can't remember exactly. I would always normally discuss with the other colleagues involved in supporting a patient at the time, which would have been the nurses and Dr Chang. But it would be my decision rather than saying anyone else decided to take the tube out.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. You've then noted your impression. Take us through that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I've already mentioned that -- and I didn't write that down -- I couldn't think of a natural disease process that had caused [Baby I] to suddenly deteriorate so rapidly and then to recover so well with some support. So from the history I'd given of [Baby I]'s developing distress, crying just before midnight, and then rapidly deteriorating, I'd assumed something had upset her, made her unhappy, and then she'd suffered generalised lung collapse, and that's very stiff, small-volume lungs, due to her distress and her crying.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When anyone cries, you breathe out, you breathe out forcibly when you're crying. And [Baby I] had had a short period, I was told, of -- and I wasn't there so I don't know exactly what it was like -- unusual cry, seeming in distress and then rapidly deteriorating. So something had upset her.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We knew she was hungry because she was not being fed into her tummy, she was being fed intravenously, awaiting investigations in Liverpool. But hunger doesn't usually -- does not cause someone to suddenly be in severe pain, appear to be in pain, and then rapidly deteriorate. So it appeared to be something else rather than just being hungry.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Once you've got distressed and breathed out heavily, your lungs can collapse down a bit because they're getting smaller. And because [Baby I] had chronic lung disease of prematurity, it would be more difficult then to re-inflate the lungs. That's what I'd supposed had happened, but I must admit I wasn't sure what had happened to cause that collapse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there anything on the X-ray that we've just looked at to support that suspicion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... No, because -- I mean, my suspicion was that she'd cried in distress and her lungs had become much smaller and then it was difficult for her to breathe.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But by the time the X-ray was taken she'd been given breathing support, an endotracheal tube had been put down, and her lungs on that X-ray we've just seen are reasonably well expanded, but it was taken after the event that caused her collapse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You've marked "No changes on X-ray". What's that last word on that note, please? So "impression" and you have taken us through it, but I think it says at the end, "CXR" and does that say "likely"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh, sorry:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "From the history, vigorous movements once resuscitated and no changes on chest X-ray."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it's:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Likely generalised lung collapse."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I was trying to retrospectively work out what had happened to her, so it's likely that there'd been general collapse of her lungs, meaning just becoming smaller because she'd been very distressed with crying and that had caused her lungs to become small. And the smaller the lungs are -- like a balloon, the smaller it is, the harder it is to blow up and a moderately large balloon is easier to blow up, so I had assumed that was why she had got into so much trouble. But I admit, I was struggling to understand exactly what had happened to [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. If we move on to your plan, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No septic screen at present."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If infection had caused the collapse in [Baby I] then she would need a septic screen, blood samples and probably also a lumbar puncture to look for possible infection and to start antibiotics. All of that is moderately distressing for a baby. We do it because it's important to treat infection, but for a baby like [Baby I] that had just suffered a severe episode of distress that had caused her to collapse and almost stop breathing, I didn't want to undertake other investigations that I didn't think were necessary at the time, to cause her further distress and therefore perhaps a further similar collapse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I didn't think she was likely to be infected because if she was and it had caused her collapse, she would not have recovered so quickly and looked so vigorous and active within minutes of being overwhelmed by infection. So I thought we would not do a septic screen:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Instead offer sucrose if distressed."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that's sugar, really, sugar water. Sounds strange. It's a common practice we do with neonates, to give a little bit of water -- even babies who are not being fed into their tummy,
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: like [Baby I], a little bit of water just trickled on to the tongue or inside the cheek, the sugar gives a little -- it seems to give a little enjoyment to the babies, it's thought it can release natural endorphins -- that's like morphine, opiates in the brain -- which soothes babies and calms them down. We do that if we're going to put cannulas into babies or take bloods from babies as a form of pain relief and to settle a baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So I felt that given [Baby I] had had this period of sudden distress and rapidly collapsed that we'd try to overcome any distress or discomfort, if she was displaying any, by giving her sucrose and not actually undertaking further investigations at this time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. Is this if (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I felt a bit uncomfortable about [Baby I] because I didn't understand properly why she had collapsed. So if she did it again we thought, fine, in that case will just have to ventilate her and continue ventilating her and probably -- in brackets it says "with paralysis", assuming she was fighting the ventilation like she had previously.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did that conclude your contact with [Baby I] on that particular occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And do you recall how [Baby I] was when you left her?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She seemed stable, she was -- the tube had been -- the endotracheal tube had been taken out. I think she was in air. I have tried to look at her observations at this time between midnight and 1 o'clock in the morning and I don't think they were recorded, not on the standard observation charts. They might be somewhere in her record, I haven't been able to see them, but I think the nurses were rather busy helping [Baby I] at this time rather than doing the routine hourly observations.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But I think she was in air, she wasn't needing any other respiratory support, and she seemed settled. She was sucking her dummy, looking like a well baby when I left. Otherwise I shouldn't have left.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Any significance in sucking a dummy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's an indication of a baby who -- ill babies don't suck their dummy, they're very quiet and lethargic. A baby sucking a dummy is part of a normal reflex. It may indicate a hungry baby, but [Baby I] was behaving normally at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were you content to leave her at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, in the care of the nurses and Dr Chang.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. Were you called back that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unfortunately, I was. Probably less than half an hour later after I'd got home I had another phone call that [Baby I] had collapsed again, so I quickly returned to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could go, please, to tile 149. Just click behind that, please. So that suggests your return at 01.23, doctor. Is that consistent with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember exactly what time I returned. I think in the notes that we'll look at in a moment, written in retrospect as usual, I think I thought it was about 01.25, so given a couple of minutes, that's fine.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. Let's go to that note, please, 193, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So written at 02.15, as you rightly said:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Called back to the hospital at 01.18 and arrived at 01.25."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. This is [Baby I]'s condition now at the time I'd arrived.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall what you were told when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That [Baby I] had done the same thing, that she'd -which I presume meant she'd had an episode of distress and rapidly deteriorated again and her oxygen levels had dropped, her heart rate had dropped, and the nurses looking after her and Dr Chang -- and I don't know what order, they were all there when I got in again -- had had to support her breathing again. Dr Chang had put another endotracheal tube in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Again, as you arrived, do you remember the scene as you arrived, that second occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, roughly. The nurses and Dr Chang were all around [Baby I], supporting her. She was receiving chest compressions this time. She wasn't -- she had been receiving chest compressions for a short while after her first collapse but she wasn't receiving those chest compressions when I arrived after that first collapse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: After the second collapse the chest compressions were in progress as well as [Baby I] being ventilated through her endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You told us Dr Chang was there. Do you remember any of the other staff who were present?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, the same two staff nurses.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You remember that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They were there, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember what others may have been doing when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember precisely what everyone was doing, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Let's go back to your note. So as you said, you have noted what you found; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Intubated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Intubated, Neopuff ventilation, chest compression."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You then noted "poor perfusion"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And again you've made an entry about mottling.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Mottling and purple and white in colour."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you describe it to us again, what you saw on this occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the second occasion it was all over [Baby I], the whole of her body was affected, indicating poor perfusion.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. You've then put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Question mark] good air entry/chest movement."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's something you'd have seen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. By the question mark, it means not clear that there was good air entry or chest movement.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we changed the Neopuff device, which I think has been described for the court in the past.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, it has, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Changed over to a bag, just putting a collapsable/compressible bag on to the endotracheal tube. It's an alternative way of providing ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Sometimes with the bag you can, it depends how hard you press, achieve higher pressure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And in brackets, you've written what, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Changed bag with overriding [I think it's 'of'] blow-off valve."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: On this bag there's a little valve which prevents you producing too high a pressure when you squeeze the bag, but because at this stage I was concerned we weren't actually moving any air and oxygen in and out of [Baby I]'s lungs, you can override the valve just by putting your finger on it and it allows you to achieve a higher pressure to inflate the lungs better.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then you've revisited in your next note the chest movement. Could you tell us what you have noted there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Arrow] [meaning 'led to'] good chest movement and air entry, but crackles on inspiration."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So using the bag and higher pressure, we were now getting air and oxygen in and out of [Baby I]'s lungs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Despite that, though, the saturations weren't good at 70%.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the air is going in and out but the level of oxygen in the blood is not recovering; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's still low, it's in the 70s. And worryingly, even more worryingly, [Baby I]'s pulse rate was low at 50-60; it should be well over 100 in a baby of [Baby I]'s age.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that "starting"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Showing." "Showing 2:1", really. It's 2:1. It's:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "2:1 or 3:1 heart block."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we only know that because [Baby I] had a heart rate monitor measuring the electrical activity of her heart on the screen and 2:1 and 3:1 just means -- if I step back a bit, when you look at the electrical heart rate trace, you see a little blip at the beginning followed by a larger deviation and that's electricity going around the heart as it beats. That little blip at the beginning should be followed by the larger deviation of electricity and in [Baby I] she was having little blips with no main electrical activity following it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And sometimes she would have two little blips before you would get the main electrical contraction of the heart, sometimes she'd have three little blips. All that means is abnormal heart response. So she was showing an abnormal, slow rhythm.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. You have then noted that she was given repeated adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have told us before the purpose of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's to stimulate the heart to contract more forcibly --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there any significance (inaudible: distorted) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Erm, when --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just pause for a moment, doctor.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know what's happened.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was a remote microphone playing up.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I asked you about the significance, if any, of the adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, it's quite worrying when you need to use adrenaline in any patient because it means they've collapsed and their heart isn't functioning properly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It could be anything from not functioning at all to not functioning properly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In [Baby I]'s case her heart was still beating but abnormally slowly with very poor circulation from the purple mottled colour she was showing and with abnormal rhythms on the electrical tracing, the ECG, that we were recording.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the adrenaline is to stimulate the heart. It speeds the heart up, but it also causes the heart muscle to contract more forcibly. But when you need to use adrenaline, it means the patient is very ill.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can see there reference to:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Repeated adrenaline at 10ml per kilogram saline bolus."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And also a dose of bicarbonate (overspeaking) is that to reduce the acidity of the blood (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right. When there's poor circulation acid builds up, so bicarbonate helps to counter that. If acid builds up then a patient doesn't respond as well to adrenaline. These are all drugs used in the resuscitation of very ill patients.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You've explained to us the remaining in 3:1 heart block and the rate, is that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Still staying slow at about -- the squiggle means "approximately" -- 60.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "No response..." -- could you read the rest of that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No response to 100 [micrograms] of atropine."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It's a drug we occasionally use in cardiac arrest or severe illness situations to try and speed the heart up, but unfortunately [Baby I] didn't respond to that:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Also no response to 0.3ml/kg of 10% calcium gluconate."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Again, calcium is a drug we occasionally use in cardiac arrest. It helps to -- it also helps to improve heart contraction, or that's the intention of it anyway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Given 0.2ml of 1:1,000 adrenaline."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just trying a stronger -- the normal adrenaline we use is called 1:10,000. We'd gone up tenfold to 1:1,000 at times to try and get some response from [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we can scroll down a little, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Temporarily, [Baby I]'s heart did respond:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Heart rate [that's an arrow up] [increased] to 120-130 and narrow complexes with ST elevation."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The ST elevation is a -- isn't a very reliable sign just on a heart rate monitor, it sometimes means some ischaemia, lack of blood getting to the heart. But the ECG heart rate changes are bizarre and variable when you're in a cardiac arrest situation. It just means the heart isn't working, really.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But the heart rate had increased from around 60 or less up to 120, which is a more normal heart rate, but sadly, only temporarily.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard that from time to time a resuscitation will be paused for those sort of things to be checked.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that one of those points in the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At the bit where we're talking about -- yes -- once you see a heart rate change you then check the pulses to see whether you can feel a pulse. If someone's pressing on the chest that should give you a pulse hopefully so you have to pause the pressing on the chest and you feel either the arm, the brachial pulse, or the groin, the femoral pulse, to see if there's a spontaneous pulse, [Baby I]'s own pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think that probably introduces us to the next entry, which confirms that the brachial and the femoral pulses were palpable.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, you could feel a pulse. For the first time during the resuscitation [Baby I] was producing her own pulses, so the heart was recovering slightly. So we stopped the chest compressions at 01.45 --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You put a note there saying resuscitation had started — is that at --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At 1.16, yes, half an hour. And 29 minutes into the resuscitation there was a pulse palpable. The saturations were fairly good at 95% to 100%, but this is with [Baby I] being ventilated with, it would have been likely, 100% oxygen. But she's still remained mottled and poorly perfused. And because of the poor perfusion, but she now has her own pulse back, she was given some saline to try and improve the circulation, to give a little bit more volume into her blood system.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that's the next entry, we can see, "given" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "2ml of 10ml per kilogram..."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Sorry, given the second because she'd had one dose before, so given the second bolus of 10ml per kilogram saline.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then, unfortunately, 5 minutes later can you take us through the entry (overspeaking), please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Despite the brief improvement, and this was just an improvement with the heart returning, [Baby I] was still not breathing by herself, she was needing to have the ventilation done for her. But 5 minutes later, her heart rate dropped down to 70, saturations dropped, and we no longer could feel any brachial or femoral pulse, so she'd lost her own pulse. So therefore cardiac compressions were restarted.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that's -- just checking your note -- 5 minutes after you initially found something?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There's then another dose of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, further adrenaline given, but without any response, in other words, without an increase in heart rate or any pulses becoming palpable when we weren't pressing on her chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then given more atropine. So we're going through the same drugs again, really, to try and hopefully get another improvement out of [Baby I], but so far the only improvement we had was a pulse, no breathing from [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Does that then say:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Increase in heart rate on monitor"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unfortunately, the last word on the line after adrenaline is blocked out by our pagination, but looking at the next line, is that "increase in HR"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, right. Yes, behind the red number is:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Temporary increase in heart rate on the monitor to about 100 for 2 or 3 minutes, before falling back again to 40 to 50."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then that same heart block that you've explained to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I've lost it on my screen, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I've lost it on mine too. It's back again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Bottom right-hand corner where we see in red J14923 and under that it reads:
"Temporary increase in heart rate on monitor to around 100 for only 2 to 3 minutes before falling to 40 to 50 with heart block 2:1 or 3:1."
So you repeat that:
"No pulse palpable, spontaneous during the" --
If we can carry on down, please. It continues -- it describes the duration of the second episode. So what you just said is the situation during the course of that second attempt —
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. We didn't get a return of -- spontaneous return of [Baby I]'s own pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does that say --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good chest movement and air entry with ventilation."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the ventilation -- at the beginning it was difficult to get chest movement, that's why I added the bag and the high pressure. But throughout this part of the resuscitation, only because nurses and doctors were giving the ventilation to [Baby I], her chest was moving well, but she wasn't breathing herself and she was no longer producing any spontaneous pulse herself. And her parents had arrived by this stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it's to them, presumably, that the next paragraph refers when you talk about explaining [Baby I] was not responding?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The resuscitation was still continuing, although I've written all this in retrospect, just after this has ended, but:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Explained that [Baby I] wasn't responding to this resuscitation that we were giving her and although her heart was beating, there was no effective circulation."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So we had no pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Your next entry is at 02.10 and the heart is down to 40 per minute; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right, yes, "No pulse".
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In brackets "Heartbeat..."?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Audible." If we listen with a stethoscope we can hear the heart beating but not strongly enough to produce any pulse that you could feel.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And therefore not strong enough to pump blood around (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's without cardiac --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, there was no pulse when we weren't giving cardiac compression.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "No respiratory effort"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby I] wasn't making any respiratory effort, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You then comment on her pupils.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, her were pupils fixed and dilated. That means when you look at the pupils, the black part of the eye, they were very wide, which is a bad sign. It's a sign of lack of oxygen to the brain. In itself that's not a reason to stop resuscitation because occasionally medication drugs can cause that, but not adrenaline, adrenaline causes very small pupils. But that was a worrying sign as well. But the main worrying sign was we'd been trying to help [Baby I] with vigorous resuscitation for not quite an hour, 50 minutes or so, and she still had no pulse of her own, she wasn't making any breathing effort of her own, and because we tried so many doses -- I think eight doses of adrenaline -- it's usually futile to continue. In fact, it's often futile to continue up to eight doses of adrenaline, but we had had a brief response for 5 minutes in the middle of the resuscitation, only to the extent of [Baby I] having a pulse, not breathing by herself. That's why we carried on for a rather long resuscitation but decided at this stage we needed to stop.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You then noted that [Baby I] was extubated and handed to her parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then a short while later, at 02.30, you have noted that you examined [Baby I] while in her parents' arms.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There was no respiratory movement, no heart sounds, you commented again on her pupils and you have indicated that [Baby I] has passed away?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It was later that morning, not at 02.30 in the morning, that I phoned the coroner's officer to report [Baby I]'s death because I didn't know or couldn't understand why she had collapsed and died.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Let's just go then, for the sake of completeness, please, to tile 227.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Am I allowed to comment on the (inaudible: coughing) coroner on the post-mortem cause of death?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think we're going to hear, thank you, from a pathologist.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we can just scroll down to your entry there. That's 9.40, later that same morning, and you report -- you have named the coroner's officer there. Can you explain -- can you just tell us what you've noted there, what you told the coroner?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Explained to the coroner's officer that cannot assign a clear cause of death, probable coroner's post-mortem, but he will check with the coroner."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We asked the coroner -- we report deaths to the coroner. It's the coroner's decision whether to undertake a post-mortem to try to determine the cause of death. That's why I say probably I felt [Baby I] needed a post-mortem, but it's the coroner's decision. So at this stage I could only say she probably will have a post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. We know that a post-mortem indeed followed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you happen to recall where you were when you informed the coroner's officer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I don't. I would have been somewhere in the hospital, I don't know exactly where, when I phoned.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Probably on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Does that note reflect your view of the situation at the time you contacted the coroner?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Gibbs. I have no more questions, but if you could wait there for a moment, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Could we put up tile 110, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If we scroll down a little bit towards the bottom of the page, and Dr Gibbs, if you follow it down. Can you see it says just above plan, "Generalised lung collapse"?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The entry says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Generalised lung collapse. Very swift."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that "small-volume lungs"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Very stiff small-volume lungs."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Very stiff small-volume lungs due to distress and crying."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was my presumption at why [Baby I] had collapsed, but I wasn't sure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. Next, I would be grateful if we could go to the notes -- they're not in the carousel, but they're at 14927.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There was a debrief, wasn't there, after [Baby I]'s death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll have a look at what appeared there, please. This is something which is generally held, isn't it, after there'd been a death; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And this took place on 9 November 2015.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, just after -- 2 weeks after [Baby I]'s death.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It says "11.00 debrief meeting" and then is there a list of the people who were present for the debrief.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It has the Reverend John Kingsley; is he the hospital chaplain?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, he'd started to attend the debrief meetings because we'd had a sudden increase in deaths in 2015, despite nothing else changing, clinical practices hadn't changed, staffing levels hadn't changed from previous years.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then we've got Staff Nurse Ashleigh Hudson?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Staff Nurse Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. The other person that ought to have been there is registrar Dr Rachel Chang, but we try to arrange these meetings when people are available. It depends how busy she was and whether she was on the shift this day. And this is already 2 weeks after the event, so sometimes we have to hold a debrief meeting without all the relevant people there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you looking through what it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Discussed briefly overall cause of illness since prem delivery."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Discussed episodes of sudden" -- is that cardio (overspeaking)?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Cardiorespiratory.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "... cardiorespiratory deterioration [and then] the week before death, then again at the time of death."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And then it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Seemed fine and stable prior to episodes of sudden collapse."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that a reference to the sudden collapse on the night of the 22nd into 23 October, the night you were there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But it's... We'd been reviewing briefly -- we weren't doing a detailed review of the extensive notes in [Baby I], we were briefly reviewing her history, so we had looked back over the collapses she'd had previously. I can't recall, because it would have been my opinion together with the two staff
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: nurses, so whether we were talking just about the collapses on the night of the 23rd or the previous collapses, I can't be sure. I hadn't been involved in those previous collapses directly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then you've got, is that "except" -- what's the next word? "Accept [something] removing"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "That."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Accept that removing ETT after first collapse might not have helped."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that acknowledging that there's a possibility it might have been better to leave it in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it says "might". The reason it's might, not that they did not help, is it was unclear why [Baby I] had collapsed, so depending on why she'd collapsed, keeping the endotracheal tube in might have helped. But as I've explained, I couldn't understand any natural disease process that had affected [Baby I] that had caused her to collapse and recover so quickly that required the endotracheal tube remaining in. And [Baby I] was behaving as though she did not need an endotracheal tube by fighting ventilation and being very active.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. With hindsight, looking at all options, it might have been better to leave it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, because my plan was if [Baby I] had collapsed again we would put the tube in and keep it in and of course I wasn't expecting half an hour later, after I got home, to be called back because she had collapsed again.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then it says -- and this goes on to what you have told us about:
