blocks.text: You may recall his Lordship invited us to help the jury with what that actually meant when it was read out.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you just help us with that in the context of this particular X-ray and what had happened to [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Simply there was no air in the biliary tree, in other words there was no air -- the absence of air in the biliary tree is a normal finding.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What is the biliary tree?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The biliary tree is the bit underneath the liver where the gall bladder -- and the gall bladder drains from the liver into the intestine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So is it part of the digestive process?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's part of the digestive process, yes. So it's the tube that connects the pancreas, the gall bladder, yes, and where the -- yes, that's what it is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Falciform ligament?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm not sure -- it's simply saying that there's no air there, that's all.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So is this in the context of investigating whether there's some digestive abnormality to which the vomiting might be attributable?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, in this particular case they were concerned about necrotising enterocolitis on a number of occasions. If you have a baby with suspected necrotising enterocolitis, one of the serious things, serious findings, is that you get perforation of the intestine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you get perforation of the intestine, you get leakage of air into the abdomen and that air may be found on the abdominal Xray. Therefore the absence of this air means there is no air. Therefore you cannot explain any of this on the basis of any kind of intestinal catastrophe.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. So dealing with [Baby I]'s collapses and her vomiting at 16.30 on 30 September, just to put this into context, can we go back to the paper documents, please, behind divider 12 at the beginning. It should be the second page in, which is 14715.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do we see there, Dr Evans, that hourly observations of [Baby I] had begun at 3 pm, 15.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do we see that [Baby I] had no respiratory support?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Her sats were 96 and 95, 93, 100% in oxygen, between 15.00 and 20.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In air, actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Sorry, yes, in air.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In air, yes. Normal oxygen saturations, not requiring oxygen, extra oxygen.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. So what conclusions did you draw so far as the episodes of desaturation and the episode of vomiting was concerned at 16.30 and 19.00 hours on that first occasion, 30 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The conclusion I drew was that something had happened out of the blue. If she had been sickening for an infection or one of the complications that one gets with premature babies, I would have expected over the previous hour or two or three or more, for instance, for her to need a little bit of oxygen support. I would have expected her heart rate to change, to increase.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There might have been drops in her oxygen saturation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There was none of this. So she was entirely stable right until she suddenly collapsed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: My conclusion was that she had collapsed as a result of some kind of event and, looking at the X-rays and looking at the clinical pattern, my opinion was that [Baby I] had been subjected to an infusion of air, in other words air had been injected into her stomach. If you have a large infusion of air into the stomach that interferes with the ability of the diaphragm to move up and down, therefore that interferes with your breathing.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Anything that interferes with your breathing will quickly reduce your oxygen to your tissues, reducing your oxygen saturation, and then reducing your heart rate. In [Baby I]'s case she had a large -- what was described as a large vomit.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The large vomit was therapeutic because by vomiting, she was reducing the pressure in her abdomen and therefore making it easier for her to breathe. And on top of that, as we described a few minutes ago, she had a nasogastric tube in and someone aspirated "air +++", three pluses. So therefore that would have reduced the abdominal pressure even more, and this is what led to her recovery.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, all right. Just dealing with the issue of splinting of the diaphragm, if we go to the X-ray, please, at tile 78, what does that show us?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Now, I'm not a radiologist, but that is the diaphragm, that area there (indicating). Below the diaphragm you've got loads and loads of air in the whole of the intestine. There's lots and lots of air everywhere. I think that's the stomach (indicating) -- I'm not too sure if it's the stomach or a large bowel, actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think Dr Arthurs told us that that was part of the bowel.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I think so. Anyway, we've got a large amount of air, and Dr Arthurs knows much more about this than me, in the whole of the abdomen. If you have air in the abdomen, you know, that's the whole of the abdomen all round there (indicating), that diaphragm would normally move up and down. But if there's a lot of air there, in the abdomen, it cannot move up and down effectively, and that will lead to the oxygen desaturation, which would have led to the collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other point I make here is that these are the lungs -- and it's not the best quality X-ray, that's not a criticism, but there's no sign of lung collapse and there's no sign of pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So in your opinion, just to be absolutely clear, so far as [Baby I]'s desaturations on 30 September was concerned, your view was the cause of that was?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Splinting of the diaphragm caused by an injection of air into the stomach, increasing pressure within the abdomen, interfering with diaphragm movement and therefore causing her collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, all right. Can we move on to 13 October, please, Dr Evans. Just to remind us all, this is the occasion when [Baby I] was found collapsed in nursery 2 --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- in the early hours of the morning.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This was at about 03.20 on the morning of the 13th.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The apnoea alarm hadn't sounded, as we heard from Ashleigh Hudson.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But her saturations and heart rate had both dropped and she required some resuscitation, including adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She needed an awful lot of resuscitation, actually, and her condition -- this is event 2. Her condition on this occasion was much worse than on event 1. Her heart rate had dropped, had recorded values of 50, which is very low for a baby, it should be 120 or more. Her oxygen saturation was very low, had dropped to 53, that's extremely low and placing her life at risk. And I also noted that at one stage they were unable to detect a heart rate. So therefore, if they were unable to detect the heart rate it suggests that her heart was not pumping normally.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So the resuscitation they introduced was incredibly vigorous, adrenaline on three occasions and, as earlier, bicarbonate, dextrose and saline boluses. They then did an abdominal X-ray and this was -- I'm sure we can see it, it shows lots of air in the stomach and in the intestines.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just to remind us of the degree of breathing support or not that [Baby I] was getting in the immediate time before this collapse, if we go in the paper documents, please, to the second divider in section 12. The documents with the blue 2 in the right-hand corner.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If we find the observation chart that's numbered J14719, we can see that as from 7 am on 11 October, [Baby I] had been having her temperature checked only.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There'd been no checks of her heart or of her respirations. Is that right, first of all?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what the statement says, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's what the chart says, sorry.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It does. We then see, reading across, that although somebody hasn't written in 12 October, it should be written in between 21.30 and 09.30?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Which are the fifth and sixth columns from the right respectively. And it would follow that 13 October, in other words the time immediately before this collapse, begins in the very final column on that page?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So at 01.30, we can see that [Baby I] was on no respiratory support. She was in air; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, where?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We're looking at the very final column on page 14719.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right, okay. Yes, she's in air, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then immediately after the collapse is the first column on the next page, 14720. We see that she'd been intubated, her respiration level being marked with a cross in circles; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That she was on 15-minute observations, which then went to half an hour and then in due course went to an hour?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So looking at the collapse, the fact that she was on no support at the time and looking at the nature of the collapse, what conclusions did you reach as to the cause for [Baby I]'s collapse at 03.20 that morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I came to a similar conclusion to event 1 because, again, the collapse was unexpected, she was stable before all of this, but it was much more serious on this occasion, it required even more robust resuscitation, but there had been some kind of incident where her breathing and heart rate had been compromised. I think there's an X-ray somewhere.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There is.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That shows again lots of gas in the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Sorry, it was on my screen, I've just lost it.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's about 4.30 that morning, the X-ray. I'll just find it. If Mr Murphy could go to [Baby I] 2, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Tile number 80. It's an X-ray at 04.25 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So just by reference, perhaps using the mouse that you have there, Dr Evans, can you, in short form, talk us through what you're talking about?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My mouse has stopped working.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Right. So this X-ray shows the chest and about half of the abdomen, so again we've got --
I think we know the lungs --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The lungs are there (indicating), they're okay. And here (indicating)you've got loads and loads of air in the intestines. Lots and lots more air than you'd anticipate, than you'd expect normally. That's all one can say, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. You've already told us that your opinion was it was in effect that air that had caused this desaturation; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Something had occurred to interfere with her breathing, so again we're back to splinting the diaphragm. So that is -given what had happened on event 1, we're seeing a similar pattern of sudden onset deterioration, from which she recovered following robust resuscitation, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It may be that you'll be asked in more detail to look at the surrounding circumstances, but so far as you were concerned, was there any suggestion in the surrounding circumstances preceding or indeed immediately succeeding this incident that would give cause to believe that there were some benign cause for what happened to [Baby I] at that time on the 13th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, up until, you know, the time she suddenly deteriorated, she appeared to be well. She was in the nursery, the lights were down, as we heard. It was early morning. A nurse had -- she was on monitoring.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A nurse had moved away to prepare milk, I think. So this was a nice, well prem baby, simply being looked after in a neonatal
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: unit until she would have been well enough or big enough to go home. So there weren't any warning signs as far as one could tell that would have alerted any nurse or doctor to the possibility that [Baby I] would suddenly have collapsed during the early hours of the morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Now, moving on to the third event, which was between 5 am and 7.45 am or so the following day, 14 October. I'm now turning, Dr Evans, to your subsequent report of 25 March 2019.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If Mr Murphy could help us, please, and we go to the third sequence of events for [Baby I]. Tile 70 first of all, please. This is the marker for the first event on the 14th. The second event is at 07.45 and the marker or the record of that is in Dr Neame's notes at tile 115. What conclusions did you draw about this collapse, please, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Similarly to events 1 and 2, that again she had stabilised following event 2, but then on this occasion her abdomen had become very distended, areas of discolouration. The examination noted:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Abdomen firm and distended."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So again, that her condition had deteriorated as a result of some kind of event that had interfered with her breathing and I really came to a similar conclusion to the one I did for events 1 and 2.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In the report I said -- it states:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "The events of the early hours of 14 October are also suspicious and suggestive of inappropriate care, most likely due to the perpetrator injecting a large volume of air into the stomach via a nasogastric tube."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that was my opinion at that time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just taking that opinion and looking at alternatives, so far as infections or anything like that were concerned, could you see in the records any suggestion of a sort of benign explanation which could account for what happened to [Baby I] when she collapsed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was no evidence of it. Secondly, her response to resuscitation is not what one would expect if she had an infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Infections tend -- as a result of infection, babies tend to recover over a number of days, not over a matter of minutes or
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: an hour or so or less. So there was no sign of any other complication. There was no collapsed lung, there was no pneumothorax, there was no infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Again, I think we had X-rays that showed this astonishing large amount of -- volume of air.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. If anyone wants to refer to it, and if Mr Murphy could quickly put it on to the screen, please, it's tile 129.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's start with tile 85, which is after the earlier of the two collapses. This is an X-ray taken at 06.05, following the collapse at about 5 am.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, here we are, this is lungs as before, no collapse. That's the diaphragm there (indicating). The whole of this is the abdomen (indicating) and it is absolutely full of air. And this degree of air would be likely to cause interference with breathing. If you look here, I think this here is a nasogastric tube (indicating), so she did have a nasogastric tube in her stomach at the time. So again, I formed a view similar to the view I'd formed regarding events 1 and 2.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The X-ray taken later that morning was taken at just after 8 o'clock. It's tile 129, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think the report suggests that it's a similar picture to the one that had been seen earlier in the day.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is that a fair summary?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that's a fair comment, actually, yes, lots of air.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The jury already have that evidence in the sequence of events in the form of Dr Wright's report. And of course Professor Arthurs has already given us his view.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So moving on, if we may, please, to [Baby I]'s final collapse and her untimely death.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And going back to your original -- your fuller report, please. Dr Evans, can you talk us through, please, what in your view was the cause for [Baby I]'s final collapse and death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I thought on this occasion that she was subjected to an infusion of air again. But on this occasion, I think it was
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: more likely that the air was injected into the blood circulation. Going back over the previous few days, she'd been stable, she'd stabilised, she was recorded as breathing spontaneously in air, her oxygen saturations were 96% or higher. In other words, a very stable, well baby. We've talked about rooting, so that's fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But suddenly, she collapses, as we heard from Dr Gibbs' evidence this morning.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, okay. As we have with the others, if we may, let's go to the paper documents to remind ourselves of the picture. So this is divider 4. Right at the beginning of divider 4 is the observations chart, which is page 15034.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We're still in section 12, are we?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We're in section 12, the fourth divider. The first page is the one we were looking at before. I think we've looked at it at some stage anyway. It's the 20th, the 21st and 22 October --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- and it runs through on the following page, 15035, to 23.00 hours on 22 October.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And of course, 23.00 hours was left blank for the reasons given to us in evidence by Ashleigh Hudson.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But just concentrating on the general picture, we've got heart rate, respiration rate, temperature, saturations in air, and the position of a probe.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They're all features that are recorded in this data on two separate pages?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What is the general picture so far as whether or not [Baby I] was a well child or whether there was something to suggest there was something wrong?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] from these results was a very stable baby. Her heart rate was around 140, which is normal for a baby of this
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: age. Her respirations were 40 to 50, which is normal for a baby this age.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Oxygen saturations, she was on continuous monitoring, but we've got four values here, 100, 95, 97, 96, can't get better than that, so despite being known to have chronic lung disease she was not needing additional oxygen, so that's very satisfactory. And she was in air, in other words 21% oxygen. So this was a stable baby from this account.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: By this time, of course, she was several weeks old, she was about 1.8 kilograms from memory, so she was now a good size.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We heard from Ashleigh Hudson about [Baby I]'s relentless cry at about the time of the first collapse at about midnight. And then that being repeated on the second occasion.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I think the relentless crying from Ashleigh Hudson's opinion was on the first part of the --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Both collapses, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So Ashleigh Hudson's evidence was very moving because nurses and doctors know what one would call a normal cry sounds like because babies will cry if they're hungry, they'll cry if you take blood tests from them because it hurts. But it was clear that this was a very abnormal, different kind of cry, and I would have interpreted that cry as the cry of a baby who was in pain and a cry of a baby who was severely distressed. In other words, this baby was in severe pain from the description we heard from the local team last week and this morning. That is an extremely disturbing phenomenon. We heard it in previous cases about this abnormal cry. So there was no obvious explanation why she was crying relentlessly and it was very loud. That's what we heard.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because there wasn't -- it wasn't as if somebody was shoving needles into her or, you know, causing her harm at all. So this was an extremely disturbing phenomenon.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And thus you concluded, so far as the causes of her collapse and ultimately her death were concerned, that was the result of what?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think she was a victim of having air injected into her blood circulation. This also probably explains her crying, her distress, and the failure of the medical team the second time round to save her life.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Evans. Would you wait there, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

Dr Evans, do you agree that [Baby I] was in general a very poorly baby regardless of the particular events that we're looking at?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't, actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree that she had recurrent episodes of abdominal distension regardless of the events that we're looking at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree that she had recurrent desaturations regardless of the events we're looking at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree there were periods when she had infection or suspected infection and received treatment for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree that there were periods when she had suspected NEC and received treatment for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree that she failed to put weight on as would have been expected?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Her weight gain was -- could have been a bit better, but there are explanations for that, as for the reasons that we've been discussing this morning, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you agree that the failure to put on weight could be a consequence of the cumulative problems with her ill health over time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've been looking at four events. There's an additional matter I'd like to ask you about, Dr Evans, about 23 August 2015.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I'm familiar with that event, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There are abdominal -- there's abdominal distension identified in the case of [Baby I] on that day, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And there'd been radiographs of that, haven't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm turning to just ask you this. In your first two reports, so the report on 8 November 2017 and the report on 31 May 2017, in both of those you set out that you formed the view she'd received a large bolus of air via the NGT, the nasogastric tube, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was my opinion at the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In other words, something was done to her that should not have been done to her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Something like that, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Moving to event 1, 30 September 2015, you've given evidence to us just now that in your opinion this arises because of splinting of the diaphragm by an injection of air into the stomach.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was my opinion and that was the report of the local radiologist as well in relation to the X-ray taken at the time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In relation to splinting of diaphragm. The local radiologist didn't say anything about injecting air into the stomach?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, splinting of the diaphragm, I said.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When you made your first report, your opinion was that this was due to air injected in the stomach via a syringe down the NGT, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Something like that, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you repeated that in your second report, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How much air would it take to cause that to happen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A lot, but what I can't say, and nobody can say, is how much because what you cannot do, you cannot carry out some kind of research where you inject increasing amounts of air into a baby's stomach until they either vomit or stop breathing. I mean, that would be grossly unethical and therefore you cannot carry out a research study to do that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What we do know is that normally, babies will have a small amount of air in the stomach because they swallow air, and that doesn't cause them any problems. We also know that babies who are on CPAP will get air into the stomach, and that normally doesn't cause them problems.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore, for a baby to vomit, that's the first point, means that she would have had an awful lot of air injected into the stomach. Professor Arthurs suggests more than 20ml in his evidence, but he cannot give a figure. You would need to give an awful lot of air and milk for a baby to vomit because you don't vomit air, you only vomit liquid. And of course, the nurse who applied the syringe to the nasogastric tube got out "air +++."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: My experience from these cases -- I don't know of any baby that's had more than three pluses of air ascribed to them. So therefore, she must have had an awful lot of air injected into the stomach to cause both the vomiting and the collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Do you know how long it would take for the air to be injected as you're suggesting, let's say at the time of the event at 4.30 in the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How can quickly would there be vomiting and desaturation if the abdomen has been splinted?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't say. You can't say.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Help us.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You can't say. I suspect it'd be quite quick, but again, because this is something that's incredibly rare, this is incredibly unusual, the cases that we're hearing about in this trial are incredibly unusual in their presentations. It's not possible to give an exact volume of air and it's not possible to give an exact time in terms of minutes following the injection of air that the baby would vomit. But I suspect that the greater the volume of air injected, then the earlier -- sorry, the
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's utter guesswork.

blocks.text: "'2. blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "'It is of great concern that the parents and the wider family might have been encouraged by this opinion to believe that the judge's findings might be revisited. blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think you noted the fact that the ET tube was not in the optimum position; is that right?

blocks.text: The nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I beg your pardon, yes. And was curled back on itself in the oesophagus?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can you tell us how that happens as a matter of fact?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: When, and it's usually nurses, place a nasogastric tube it obviously goes through the nostril, you push it down to what you think is the required length and the nurses have a way of measuring what they think will be the optimum length to get it into the stomach, but once you push it down the nose and to the back of the throat you have no control over where it goes and so sometimes it will loop round on itself and come back up in the oesophagus. You don't necessarily know that that's happened until you try to test it, to test to see if you can get some aspirate out to check it's in the right place. And if anyone had checked that nasogastric tube they wouldn't have got any aspirate out because it wasn't in the stomach. The other way to find out, of course, is on X-ray but you don't X-ray every time you put a nasogastric tube into a baby.

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: ventilator, they usually nurse them with their head to one side or the other and if you move the head it can sometimes push the tube down further. blocks.text: Dealing with that one first, that was the one in the afternoon and at the change of shift on 30 September.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: First of all, what conclusions did you reach as to [Baby I]'s state of health prior, immediately prior to those collapses?

blocks.text: Prior to the collapse on that day, on 30 September, [Baby I] was a well baby, giving no cause for concern. In particular, she had no respiratory symptoms and was self-ventilating in air. She was gaining weight and her collapse was sudden and unexpected.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you draw any conclusions as to why she had collapsed?

blocks.text: The usual things that one would consider in a baby that collapses suddenly, I did consider. [Baby I] did not have any of those things. She wasn't obviously suffering from an infection because it doesn't present in that way with an unexpected sudden complete collapse. So I didn't think that she was infected. I didn't think that she had a malrotation or an obstruction in her bowel to have caused her abdominal distension because that tends not to come and go. And I didn't think that she'd had signs of an intraventricular haemorrhage because again that doesn't -symptoms of that don't come and go.

blocks.text: So what we were left with was a baby with abdominal distension and collapse and I felt that the X-ray showed huge gaseous distension, so much so that the lungs were squashed, and that was easily seen on the X-ray. So it wouldn't actually take much to tip the balance to squash those lungs because they were abnormal lungs and that in turn facilitated her collapse.
